string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and one of its four municipalities. Its old city developed around a central axis that began taking shape during the Yuan dynasty. Later, the Ming and Qing dynasties added palaces, temples and ceremonial spaces along this route. The Forbidden City, completed in 1420, was the imperial residence before becoming the Palace Museum in 1925. Other historic places include the Temple of Heaven and the Summer Palace. These buildings help explain how the city changed over time. Today, visitors can explore this history alongside the streets and neighbourhoods of a modern capital.

Shanghai is a municipality on the eastern coast of China. Its history includes the establishment of Shanghai county in 1292 and the opening of the city as a treaty port in 1843. Foreign concessions developed during the nineteenth century, bringing different architectural styles and separate administrative systems. Shanghai became a special administrative city in 1927 and a municipality in 1930. Its present boundaries took shape after surrounding counties were incorporated in 1958. The city now has sixteen districts. Historic neighbourhoods preserve traces of its earlier development, while the municipality continues to connect its urban centre with suburban towns and islands.

Chongqing is a municipality in southwestern China, with an urban centre where the Yangtze and Jialing rivers meet. Mountains, valleys and rivers shape its streets and have given it the names Mountain City and River City. Chongqing opened to foreign trade in 1891 and became a city in 1929. During the war against Japan, the national government moved here and made it the wartime capital. It later became part of Sichuan province before being established as a central government municipality in 1997. Today, its territory includes both urban and rural areas, and the Yangtze remains an important link across the region.

Tianjin is a municipality in northern China, close to the Bohai Sea. Its position among rivers and near the sea helped it grow as a transport centre after the Grand Canal opened during the Sui dynasty. The canal connected waterways and supported the movement of goods between regions. In 1404, the Ming emperor established a garrison at a river crossing and gave the place the name Tianjin. This date marks the official founding of the city. Its history is closely tied to water transport and access to the coast. The municipality preserves this connection through its rivers, canal heritage and urban landscape.
